content: The term sulfa drug refers to a class of medications known as sulfonamides. This class includes several antibiotics, such as sulfamethoxazole, sulfasalazine, and sulfacetamide, among others. It is critical to differentiate sulfa drugs from other sulfur-containing compounds, such as sulfates and sulfites, which are chemically unrelated to sulfonamides and do not cause the same hypersensitivity reactions associated with sulfonamides. Sulfonamide antibiotics are used to treat a variety of infections, including Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, urinary tract infections, shigellosis, and certain protozoan infections. The sulfonamide chemical structure is also present in other medications that are not antimicrobials, such as thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, metolazone, and indapamide), sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide and glyburide), and acetazolamide. Additionally, sulfasalazine is used not only as an antibiotic but also in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease. Approximately 3% of the general population experiences adverse reactions to sulfonamide antimicrobials. Notably, individuals with HIV have a significantly higher prevalence of such reactions, estimated at around 60%. Patients who exhibit hypersensitivity to one sulfonamide antibiotic are likely to have similar reactions to other members of the class. Hypersensitivity reactions are less common with non-antibiotic sulfonamides. Although controversial, current evidence suggests that individuals with hypersensitivity to sulfonamide antibiotics do not have an increased risk of hypersensitivity to non-antibiotic sulfonamides. Two specific regions of the sulfonamide antibiotic chemical structure are implicated in hypersensitivity reactions. The first is the N1 heterocyclic ring, which is associated with type I hypersensitivity reactions. The second is the N4 amino nitrogen, which, through a stereospecific process, forms reactive metabolites that can cause either direct cytotoxicity or an immunologic response. Non-antibiotic sulfonamides lack both of these structural features. The most common manifestations of hypersensitivity reactions to sulfa drugs are rash and hives. However, there are several life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions associated with sulfa drugs, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, agranulocytosis, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and fulminant hepatic necrosis, among others.
